question: Three-class CN (HC) vs MCI vs AD classification in ADNI from MRI: diffusion white-matter indices in P-115 (Rallabandi & Seetharaman 2023; the right PDF is 1-s2.0-S1746809422005547, not the pack file) and T1-weighted structural slices in P-109 (Khatri et al. 2025). These count as one channel under the rule. Both papers also print a binary MCI vs CN accuracy.
metric: Accuracy. P-115's 0.79 is a balanced accuracy (its Table 4 labels it 'Overall Accuracy') on imbalanced classes (44/84/22). P-109's 96.81% is accuracy on near-balanced classes (315/370/390), where accuracy and balanced accuracy nearly coincide. The binary CN vs MCI figures (0.72 and 94.23%) are plain accuracies in both.

figures.P-115: Three-class balanced accuracy 0.79 (MIX_BRF, kurtosis source, tensor target), 5-fold CV, N=150. Wilson with n=150: (0.718, 0.848). If only the subjects left after P-115's balanced training draw were tested (e.g. n=96), the interval widens to (0.698, 0.860). CN vs MCI accuracy 0.72, n=128: (0.637, 0.791).
figures.P-109: Three-class accuracy 96.81% (BrainViT-L), AUC 98.05, on a random 10% hold-out of about 54,300 shuffled 2D slices from 1075 participants. The paper gives no subject count for the test set. Taking 10% of participants (n=108) as the subject-level n gives Wilson (0.916, 0.988); n=1075 would give (0.956, 0.977). MCI vs HC accuracy 94.23% (AUC 97.15%): with n=69 (10% of 685), Wilson (0.861, 0.977); with n=685, (0.922, 0.957).

matched_figure_check: Both papers print the same two contrasts, and both gaps persist: 0.79 against 96.81% for three-class, 0.72 against 94.23% for MCI vs CN. Neither paper reports the other's condition. P-109 reports no subject-level split, no diffusion input and no conventional classifier on regional features. P-115 reports no T1 slice input, no deep network and no slice-level split. On P-109's own split, most comparator networks score 87-92% three-class (ResNet-50 89.24%, DenseNet-121 87.15%, EfficientNet-B3 90.11%, Swin-T 91.18%). Only DeiT-T (79.96%) and CMT-T (74.87%) come near 0.79, and they are deep networks under the slice-level split, not P-115's condition. No matched figure reconciles the pair.
performance_validity: Checked on the sources, neither study meets the Section 3.5 exclusion as written. P-115 has no contested figure at or above 0.97 (its CN vs AD 0.96 is not contested). P-109's contested accuracy, 96.81%, is below 0.97. Its AUCs (98.05 three-class, 97.15 MCI vs HC, 98.52 AD vs HC) are at or above 0.97 on internal validation with no external cohort, but its sample of 1075 participants is not small, so the exclusion does not apply. This is the closest call among these eight pairs: P-109 shuffled its slices before a random 90/10 split, took about 50 slices per subject, and does not state subject-wise separation. That split-unit design is the one Section 3.5 names as a candidate mechanism of inflation. Under this rule it is a candidate explanation, not an exclusion.

candidate_explanations.difference: Evaluation unit and validation design: a random slice-level 90/10 hold-out with about 50 slices per subject shuffled before splitting and subject separation not stated (P-109), against subject-level 5-fold cross-validation (P-115).
candidate_explanations.quote: The images were shuffled randomly, and all experiments were carried out by splitting the data into 10 % for testing and 90 % for training. Furthermore, 20 % of the training data was used for validation. For training and testing, around 50 brain fields—axial, coronal, and sagittal—were created from each subject’s anatomy.

candidate_explanations.difference: Input representation within MRI: regional white-matter tensor and kurtosis FA/MD indices (P-115) against whole 2D T1-weighted grey-matter slices (P-109).
candidate_explanations.quote: based on white matter Gaussian diffusion (tensor) indices and non-Gaussian diffusion (kurtosis) indices

candidate_explanations.difference: Architecture: a balanced random forest with transfer between tensor and kurtosis feature sets, against a hybrid CNN-transformer. On its own split, P-109 shows that architecture moves three-class accuracy from 74.87-79.96% (CMT-T, DeiT-T) to 96.81%, but it does not show that P-115's kind of method would reach 0.79 on its data.
candidate_explanations.quote: In particular, BrainViT-L achieved 96.81 % ACC, which was 7.57 %, 3.42 %, and 4.82 % better than that of ResNet50, EfficientNet-B5, and ConvNext-T, respectively.

candidate_explanations.difference: Sample size and class balance: 150 participants split 44/84/22 against 1075 participants split 315/370/390.
candidate_explanations.quote: The structural T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and diffusion images were taken from ADNI dataset with 44 CN, 84 MCI and 22 AD patients.

candidate_explanations.difference: Training scheme and metric: equal-size class draws for training, with the remainder tested, scored by balanced accuracy (P-115), against plain accuracy on near-balanced classes (P-109).
candidate_explanations.quote: Since there is imbalance in the samples among all the groups, balanced random forest (BRF) considers equal samples from all the groups in training and rest will be assigned to test dataset.

candidate_explanations.difference: ADNI subsets: multi-shell diffusion participants (ADNI3-era protocol) against 3T T1 MPRAGE participants of unstated phase; overlap unknown.
candidate_explanations.quote: The diffusion-weighted images (DWI) were acquired with multi-shell diffusion protocols

reason: Both papers classify CN/MCI/AD from MRI in ADNI, and both the three-class figures (0.79 against 96.81%) and the binary MCI-vs-CN figures (0.72 against 94.23%) lie outside each other's 95% intervals at every test-set n considered. No matched figure reconciles them, and neither study meets the Section 3.5 exclusion as written, so all six conditions hold. The candidate explanations (slice-level random split with possible subject overlap, diffusion indices against T1 slices, forest against transformer, sample size and class balance, balanced against plain accuracy) are not shown to be sufficient by either paper; the split design in P-109 is the most material and is untested in either source.

quotes.quote: Transfer learning model using balanced random forest classifier was able to classify and predict all the groups with an overall accuracy about 0.79 using ensemble of SER and STT forests rather than individual algorithms (SER and STT). (document: 1-s2.0-S1746809422005547, scratchpad r20/conf/tlss_P115_true.txt)

Balanced accuracy of 0.79 and geometric mean of 0.78 using BRF classifier was obtained for kurtosis indices as source model and tensor indices as target and the classification accuracies of CN vs AD, CN vs MCI and CN vs MCI are 0.96, 0.72 and 0.7 respectively.

TLSS model with MIX method using source as DKI and target as DTI features achieved the highest overall accuracy and geometric mean and outperformed the other methods SER and STT for 5-fold cross-validation
We assessed 315 samples from healthy control (HC), 370 from individuals with MCI, and 390 from individuals diagnosed with AD.
The images were shuffled randomly, and all experiments were carried out by splitting the data into 10 % for testing and 90 % for training.
In particular, BrainViT-L achieved 96.81 % ACC, which was 7.57 %, 3.42 %, and 4.82 % better than that of ResNet50, EfficientNet-B5, and ConvNext-T, respectively.
the BrainViT models, particularly BrainViT-L, exhibited higher accuracy, surpassing other models, with rates of 97.13 % with 98.52 % AUC for AD/HC and 94.23 % with 97.15 % for MCI/HC classifications
Our evaluation was based on a specific ADNI dataset; however, it is crucial to verify that the model performs consistently across datasets with diverse characteristics.
